doc.what: Every datetime column the daemon writes stores a tz-aware ISO 8601 string with an explicit offset: the SQLite schema defaults and the update trigger stop emitting naive CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, the existing naive rows are backfilled as UTC, and `_rfc3339()` in api_models.py loses its naive-branch fallback (gh #31).
doc.why: The daemon's own schema contradicts its fetcher invariant: fetchers emit tz-aware UTC (INV-FETCH-1) while `DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` and the `update_content_timestamp` trigger write naive strings on every row, so `fetched_at`, `created_at` and `updated_at` are naive on nearly every row (7165, 7206 and 7206 of ~7206 on 2026-05-23) and grow more naive with every fetch cycle. `_rfc3339()` papers over it by appending `Z` to anything naive, a producer-side defect carried as a consumer-side patch. Fixing the schema is the root cause (P16); the backfill closes the historical gap; removing the naive branch makes the API's RFC3339 guarantee rest on the data rather than a guess.
decided: Schema defaults for fetched_at, created_at, updated_at and archived_at change from CURRENT_TIMESTAMP to an expression that emits a tz-aware ISO string with +00:00, matching the app-side convention datetime.now(UTC).isoformat().
The update_content_timestamp trigger emits the same tz-aware ISO string instead of CURRENT_TIMESTAMP.
A one-time, idempotent backfill rewrites every naive value in those columns (and published_at) as UTC with an explicit +00:00 offset, skipping rows that already carry an offset or Z.
`_rfc3339()` becomes a pass-through once the backfill has run: no Z append, no tzinfo check.
A new invariant INV-STORAGE-TS-1: all datetime columns store tz-aware ISO 8601 strings with explicit offset; INV-API-TS-1 and INV-FETCH-1 are preserved.
Tests: schema default and trigger emit tz-aware strings; backfill is idempotent and converts naive to UTC; _rfc3339 is a pass-through that still yields RFC3339 output.
The naive-branch removal in _rfc3339 ships only in a deploy where the backfill runs before the API serves, so no naive row can reach it.
open: How does the backfill run in production: as a migration the daemon applies at startup before serving (so one deploy carries schema, backfill and the _rfc3339 cleanup together), or as an operator-run command during a daemon-stopped window as the issue sketches?

impacted.role: declares DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP on categories, sources, source_categories, content (fetched_at, created_at, updated_at) and embeddings, plus three updated_at triggers that write CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
init_db applies schema.sql with IF NOT EXISTS and nothing else; get_db_connection opens WAL with check_same_thread=False; there is no schema version and no upgrade step

writes CURRENT_TIMESTAMP itself at 16 sites: the content INSERT's created_at/updated_at, the sources INSERT, every updated_at UPDATE, last_fetched_at, embeddings.created_at and archived_at; fetched_at and published_at are already bound as tz-aware ISO strings
_rfc3339 appends Z to naive datetimes so the API wire format stays RFC3339
reads sqlite directly and parses published_at and last_fetched_at with time.RFC3339 only; a naive or space-separated value fails the parse and is silently dropped
prismis-daemon verify, the post-deploy check that could assert zero naive rows
states the RFC3339 wire contract and documents the _rfc3339 Z-append as the mechanism

constraints.text: Every datetime field in API JSON responses MUST serialize as RFC3339 with an explicit offset; no naive timestamps on the wire. Consumers parse with time.RFC3339 (Go) or datetime.fromisoformat (Python).

Interfaces, schemas and stored data change additively; a breaking change ships with its migration or backfill in the same change. Anything that overwrites or migrates reads its target first and leaves a way back.
SQLite's ALTER TABLE cannot change a column's DEFAULT; changing an existing table's default means rebuilding the table. Triggers can be dropped and recreated freely.

content.created_at and updated_at (line 63), fetched_at (55), sources.created_at/updated_at (29-30), categories (15-16), source_categories.created_at (37) and embeddings.created_at (85) all default to CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, SQLite's naive 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' UTC string.

update_content_timestamp (and update_sources_timestamp at 98, update_categories_timestamp at 104) set updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP on every UPDATE, so even a tz-aware app-side write of updated_at is overwritten naive by the trigger.

init_db reads schema.sql and executes it; every statement is CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS, so an existing database keeps its original defaults and triggers whatever schema.sql now says. No PRAGMA user_version, no ALTER, no migration list exists anywhere in daemon/src.

The content INSERT binds created_at and updated_at as CURRENT_TIMESTAMP literals; the sources INSERT does the same (398); UPDATEs write updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP at 547, 620, 962, 993, 1004, 1061, 1071, 1081, 1138, 1165; last_fetched_at at 990; embeddings.created_at at 1596; archived_at at 1973. The schema defaults are therefore rarely the writer; the application is.
fetched_at falls back to datetime.now(UTC).isoformat(), the project's tz-aware convention ('2026-10-02T21:47:23.240383+00:00'); published_at is bound as item.published_at.isoformat().

fetched_at is stored in four historical string shapes (space or T separator, with or without +00:00); range queries wrap both sides in datetime() to compare them (#61). Live on cerebro 2026-10-02: 20025 space/naive, 2153 T/naive, 193 space/aware, 16113 T/aware, 1 space/naive without fraction.
_rfc3339 returns v.isoformat() if v.tzinfo else v.isoformat() + 'Z'; the naive branch is what keeps the wire RFC3339 for CURRENT_TIMESTAMP rows.

The TUI parses published_at with time.Parse(time.RFC3339, ...) and keeps the value only if err == nil; last_fetched_at the same at line 402. A naive space-separated string fails and is dropped without a message, so every source's last_fetched_at (46 of 46 naive on cerebro) and 149 naive published_at rows render as unset today.

Connections open with check_same_thread=False, journal_mode=WAL, busy_timeout=5000. The live database on cerebro is 700 MiB, SQLite 3.46.1, 38,485 content rows, 46 sources, 0 categories; naive counts: created_at 38485, updated_at 38485, fetched_at 22179, archived_at 11126, published_at 149; sources: created_at, updated_at, last_fetched_at 46 each.

The daemon's main entry never calls init_db; init_db is reached only by running database.py directly or by verify_chain (verify). There is no place today where the running daemon upgrades its own database.

Because the application writes CURRENT_TIMESTAMP itself at 16 sites and the triggers overwrite updated_at, changing schema.sql's defaults alone (the issue's step 1) would leave every new row naive; the producer-side fix is the 16 write sites plus the three triggers, with the defaults changed for fresh databases.

Replacing the triggers and running the backfill on an existing database needs a versioned, idempotent upgrade step the daemon runs itself before serving (PRAGMA user_version), because no mechanism exists and an operator-run script is recall-dependent; rebuilding tables to change DEFAULTs is unnecessary once no write relies on the default, so the 700 MiB database is never copied.

Backfilling to the RFC3339 'T...+00:00' shape fixes a live display defect in the TUI for free (last_fetched_at never parses today); the TUI needs no code change, and the storage.py datetime() wrappers stay correct for the single remaining shape.

question: How does the backfill run in production: as a migration the daemon applies at startup before serving (so one deploy carries schema, backfill and the _rfc3339 cleanup together), or as an operator-run command during a daemon-stopped window as the issue sketches?
answer: The operator delegated the choice to scrutiny: the design takes the startup-applied, user_version-guarded migration (the only form that guarantees the backfill precedes the _rfc3339 cleanup), and the gate's /scrutinize run is what confirms or redesigns it.

answer: The design covers all 16 storage.py CURRENT_TIMESTAMP write sites and the three triggers as the producers, binding the project's datetime.now(UTC).isoformat() convention at every site; schema.sql's defaults change for fresh databases only.

doc.purpose: Every datetime the daemon stores carries an explicit UTC offset, so the API's RFC3339 guarantee and the TUI's RFC3339 parse rest on the data instead of on a consumer-side guess; the historical naive rows are converted once, by the daemon itself, before any code that assumes the invariant can run.
doc.form:
One migration mechanism, one timestamp source, one invariant.

1. `daemon/src/prismis_daemon/database.py:9` (`init_db`) gains a versioned upgrade step after it applies `schema.sql`: it reads `PRAGMA user_version` and applies each numbered migration the database has not seen, inside one transaction per migration, then sets `user_version`. Migration 1, tz-aware timestamps: (a) `VACUUM INTO` a sibling `prismis.db.bak-tz` before touching anything, skipped if that file already exists, the way back the constitution requires; (b) drop and recreate the three `update_*_timestamp` triggers so they set `updated_at = strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%f','now') || '+00:00'`; (c) backfill every timestamp column the schema declares (content: published_at, fetched_at, created_at, updated_at, archived_at; sources: created_at, updated_at, last_fetched_at; categories: created_at, updated_at; source_categories: created_at; embeddings: created_at) with one UPDATE per column that rewrites values lacking an offset as `replace(substr(v,1,19),' ','T') || substr(v,20) || '+00:00'`, which keeps any fractional seconds and turns both the space and T shapes into RFC3339; (d) count the rows still lacking an offset across those columns and raise, rolling the transaction back, if the count is not zero. The migration list lives in `database.py` next to `init_db`, each entry a function taking the connection; a second run is a no-op because `user_version` is already 1.

2. `daemon/src/prismis_daemon/__main__.py:448` (right after `validate_llm_config(config)`, before any `Storage()` is built in any mode) calls `init_db()`, so the running daemon creates or upgrades its own database before it serves or fetches. `make init` and `verify_chain.py:102` already call `init_db` and get the upgrade for free; the Makefile `migrate` target is left as is.

3. `daemon/src/prismis_daemon/schema.sql`: every `DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` becomes `DEFAULT (strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%f','now') || '+00:00')` and the three triggers use the same expression, so a fresh database matches an upgraded one. Existing databases keep their old column defaults, which no write relies on after step 4.

4. `daemon/src/prismis_daemon/storage.py:284`'s convention becomes a module helper `utc_now_iso()` returning `datetime.now(UTC).isoformat()`, bound as a parameter at every one of the 16 sites that today write the `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` literal (the content INSERT's created_at/updated_at at 313, the sources INSERT at 398, the updated_at UPDATEs at 547, 620, 962, 993, 1004, 1061, 1071, 1081, 1138, 1165, last_fetched_at at 990, embeddings.created_at at 1596, archived_at at 1973). The trigger still fires on those UPDATEs and writes the same shape, so app-side and trigger-side agree.

5. `daemon/src/prismis_daemon/api_models.py:15` `_rfc3339` becomes `return None if v is None else v.isoformat()`, overloads kept; the comment about CURRENT_TIMESTAMP rows goes.

6. The TUI (`tui/internal/db/queries.go:155`, `:402`) changes nothing: its `time.RFC3339` parse now succeeds for every row, which also fixes the never-shown `last_fetched_at` on sources.

7. Tests: a migration test builds a database from the pre-change schema text with naive rows in every listed column in both historical shapes, runs `init_db`, and asserts zero naive values, `user_version` 1, the `.bak-tz` file present, triggers writing `+00:00` on a subsequent UPDATE, and a second `init_db` changing nothing; a storage test drives each public write path (add content, add source, mark read, update source, record fetch, archive, add embedding, feedback) against a fresh database and asserts every timestamp column it touched parses with `datetime.fromisoformat` and has `tzinfo` set; an `_rfc3339` test asserts a tz-aware input round-trips unchanged and `None` stays `None`. Each test is shown red with the corresponding change reverted.
commitments: The daemon upgrades its own database at startup through a `PRAGMA user_version`-numbered migration list in database.py; no step of this change is operator-run.

A migration that rewrites data first writes a `VACUUM INTO` backup beside the database and runs its rewrite in one transaction with a post-condition that fails startup loudly rather than serve a half-converted database.
One timestamp source for application writes: `utc_now_iso()` in storage.py, the existing `datetime.now(UTC).isoformat()` convention, at all 16 former CURRENT_TIMESTAMP sites.
Triggers stay, because the TUI updates `read` and `user_feedback` directly and relies on them for `updated_at`; they emit the RFC3339 shape with `+00:00`.
INV-STORAGE-TS-1: every datetime column stores an ISO 8601 string with an explicit offset; the migration's post-condition and the storage write test are its standing guards.
`_rfc3339` keeps RFC3339 on the wire (INV-API-TS-1) by passing tz-aware values through, with no naive branch.
sacrifices: Existing databases keep the old `DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` column defaults in `sqlite_master` (SQLite cannot alter them without rebuilding every table of a 700 MiB file); they are unreachable because every write binds a value, and the post-condition catches any that is not.
Trigger timestamps carry millisecond precision (`%f`) where application writes carry microseconds; both are RFC3339 and both parse everywhere the project reads them.
The first daemon start after deploy spends a few seconds on the backup and the backfill of ~130k cells before it serves.
`docs/architecture/boundaries.md:85` still describes the Z-append mechanism until the architecture refresh job rewrites it after the merge.
doc.risk: If the migration post-condition is wrong (a shape the rewrite does not cover) the daemon refuses to start after deploy until the shape is handled, which is loud and leaves the `.bak-tz` file and an untouched database; if a write site is missed, the storage write test is what catches it, and a missed one would reappear as a naive row the migration never sees again, breaking the TUI parse for that row only.
